title: Failure to Thrive Revealing a Pilomyxoid Astrocytoma: An Uncommon Case Report with Literature Review
case_prompt: An 11-month-old boy was referred for evaluation of poor weight gain (<3rd percentile) despite increased caloric intake over the previous 5 months. He was a full-term infant born to first-degree consanguineous parents; family history was unremarkable. Psychomotor development was appropriate. On examination he appeared pale and emaciated, with dry skin, sunken anterior fontanel, and prominent muscle wasting. His weight was 5 kg (<3rd percentile), with normal length and head circumference. He had left-eye nystagmus but no focal neurologic deficits; deep tendon reflexes and cranial nerves were normal. He was afebrile, with stable vital signs. Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count, renal and liver function tests, and electrolytes. Hormonal assays were within reference ranges (FSH 0.32 mUI/ml [1.5–14], LH 0.16 mUI/ml [1.2–10], testosterone 0.078 ng/ml, 8 AM cortisol 18.5 µg/dl [3.7–19.4], ultrasensitive TSH 2.59 mUI/l [0.27–4.2], FT4 21.8 pmol/l [12–22]). Serum tumor markers were normal (AFP 1.2 mUI/l [0–7]; HCG 6.82 ng/ml [0–7]). Brain MRI demonstrated a suprasellar mass measuring 59 × 41 × 40 mm that was isointense on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and showed homogeneous enhancement. The mass had a solid, noncalcified configuration without peritumoral edema or parenchymal infiltration, extended into the optic chiasm, retrosellar region, and right hypothalamus, and displaced the anterior and middle cerebral arteries while compressing the temporal lobes, cerebral peduncles, and anterior pons.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Considered diencephalic syndrome due to failure to thrive with neurologic sign of nystagmus pointing to hypothalamic–chiasmatic involvement — “diencephalic syndrome as an unconventional cause of failure to thrive during early childhood which is directly related to neoplasms regarding central nervous system, especially in the hypothalamus and the optic chiasm region.”  
2. Excluded systemic or endocrine causes as the initial workup showed normal blood counts, metabolic panels, and hormone levels — “Laboratory investigations embracing electrolyte levels, complete blood count, renal function panel, liver parameters, and hormonal assay were normal…”  
3. Ruled out germ cell tumor on the basis of normal AFP and HCG measurements — “Levels of AFP (alpha-fetoprotein)… and HCG (human chorionic gonadotropin)… were also within normal ranges: 1.2 mUI/l and 6.82 ng/ml, respectively.”  
4. Found craniopharyngioma less likely because the lesion was noncalcified and lacked cystic features typical of that diagnosis — “a suprasellar mass with solid and noncalcified configuration… homogeneously enhanced upon contrast administration.”  
5. Kept pilocytic astrocytoma in differential given the age and location but recognized imaging could not distinguish it from pilomyxoid astrocytoma — “differential diagnosis between PA and PMA seems to be challenging on the ground of imaging findings alone.”  
6. Confirmed pilomyxoid astrocytoma by characteristic histological features including monomorphous bipolar cells in a myxoid stroma with angiocentric arrangement and absence of Rosenthal fibers or eosinophilic granular bodies — “Rosenthal fibers and eosinophilic granular bodies were not identified…”
